newsitem.title: UK: BP makes West of Shetland find, UK offer new blocks.
newsitem.headline: BP makes West of Shetland find, UK offer new blocks.

text.p: British Petroleum Co Plc said on Monday it has discovered a third oilfield 100 miles west of the Shetland Islands off the northeast coast of Scotland.
BP said an exploration well on the Atlantic Margin encountered a "potentially commercial volume of hydrocarbons on UK Block 204/19".
BP and Royal Dutch/Shell Group each own 50 percent of the block.
Britain's Department of Trade and Industry welcomed the discovery, announcing it would offer two extra blocks north of the find for licensing in an "out of round" procedure.
BP said the well was drilled in 850 metres of water by the semi-submersible drilling rig Ocean Alliance between April 8 and June 8, 1996.
Although the well was not tested, log and core data confirmed the presence of hydrocarbons in Suilven, BP said.
BP is expected to bring its first Atlantic Margin field, Foinaven, on stream in April. The second field, Schiehallion, should be producing by mid-1998.

"This is an encouraging discovery. BP and our partner Shell need to carry out further work to establish whether the discovery is commercial," said BP's deputy chief executive of exploration Richard Olver.

"BP and Shell are also considering further exploration and appraisal options in the area. This will be greatly assisted greatly by the DTI announcement to designate and offer for licensing new blocks to the north," he added.

Energy minister Lord Fraser of Carmyllie said the discovery of Suilven completed "a hat-trick of finds west of Shetland for the BP/Shell partnership and brings with it the prospect of further discoveries."

The new blocks -- 204/14 and 204/15 -- would be offered separately for exploration and are not subject to a claim by the Faroe Islands during continuing discussions on the UK/Faroes boundary, he said.

"This new find justifies the industry's continuing faith in the prospects for the west of Shetland area and confirms our belief that there are still significant discoveries to be made in the UK Continental Shelf," Fraser said.
